thread.title: Dow Dips 180 Points as Captain Obvious Motions at China

author: Crystal Kim
title: Dow Dips 180 Points as Captain Obvious Motions at China
text:
Illustration: Michael Haddad By Crystal Kim Updated Sept. 24, 2018 2:29 p.m. ET Synchronized Sinking. Record closes and fresh peaks are yesterday’s news. All three major benchmark indexes edged lower on Monday as tariff tensions between the U.S. and China continue escalating. Meanwhile, corporate deals and strategic partnerships abound. In today’s Intraday Update, we…
•…note that the divergence between China and U.S. tech stocks is not a coincidence;
•…worry for those who stand to suffer this “unsatisfying bear market”;
•…and highlight Salesforce.com (CRM), which is rising after it announced a strategic partnership with iPhone-maker Apple.
The Bears Are Still Hungry
Mounting tensions between the U.S. and China have been the pink elephant in the room in 2018—cause for concern one day, indifference on another. On Monday, it was the latter, as all three major benchmark indexes fell. The Dow Jones Industrial Average has declined more than 180 points or 0.7% to 26,564.91, the S&P 500 has fallen 0.4% to 2916.70, and the Nasdaq Composite has dipped 0.3% to 7960.01.
Stepping back and looking at stocks’ performance so far this year makes it look as if trade has just raised a flicker of concern . But look closer. “This rolling bear market around the world has forced investors into areas of perceived safety,” writes Michael Wilson, an equity strategist at Morgan Stanley. “Specifically, that means the old barbell of growth stocks and defensive assets that has worked so well at moments of doubt during this post financial crisis period…Rising trade tensions only exacerbated this flight to the U.S.”
That is most apparent in the divergence between big U.S. tech and China’s tech stocks. Since both are considered high-quality, growth plays, it’s notable that Facebook (ticker: FB), Amazon (AMZN), Netflix (NFLX), and Alphabet (GOOGL) have collectively moved up, while Baidu (BIDU), Alibaba (BABA), Tencent (700.Hong Kong), and JD.com (JD) have edged lower since June, when trade became a bigger issue. That’s what happens in a cold war of technology .
Wilson dubs the current market an “unsatisfying bear market” in which stocks and sectors get wrecked, but the major benchmark indexes don’t see a big downturn. That is exactly what has happened at the global level. “Such an environment makes it more difficult for active managers to beat the index,” a very different set of conditions than in 2017, adds Wilson.
Perhaps that is what made hedge funds’ alpha go poof. Since June, hedge funds have erased about 2.5 percentage points of alpha, or outperformance relative to the market, “with no turn in sight yet in September,” according to Lyxor senior strategist Jean-Baptiste Berthon. Long-short stock strategies were the primary culprits, as well as the victims, says Berthon.
Newsletter Sign-up Valuations do remain a concern, but U.S. stocks could rise beyond what the fundamentals justify anyway, sending the S&P 500 above 3000, he says. That said, the recent pop in the 10-year Treasury yield suggests downside risk is more likely than upside, with rate increases on the horizon, says Wilson. U.S. stocks don’t need to weaken for this rolling bear market to conclude. Rather, international developed market stocks could mount a rally, catching up with U.S. markets. Investors who have sought safety in U.S. assets would miss out.
Midday Movers
Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) is up 2.4% to $31.75 after RBC Capital Markets initiated coverage with an Outperform rating.
Pinnacle Foods (PF) is down 0.9% to $66.56 after Jefferies downgraded it to Neutral.
Praxair (PX) is down 1.2% to $164.51. Bernstein initiated coverage with an Underperform rating.
Salesforce.com (CRM) is up 1.6% to $157.95. It announced a strategic partnership with Apple (AAPL), up 1.1% to $220.07, bringing technology like Face ID and Siri to enterprise customers.
Snap (SNAP) is up 0.8% to $9.21 after introducing a new way to visually search for products on Amazon.com (AMZN).
—Teresa Rivas
